hints: Look closely at the three descriptions given for complete, partial and low morphs. Do they blend smoothly into each other, or do they fall into separate clear-cut groups?
Think about the genetic story here - how many genes and alleles are mentioned for this trait, and what does that tell you about environmental influence compared with a trait like body mass?
walkthrough:
Picture the Three Separate Boxes**
Think of armour plating as sorting fish into three separate boxes: full cover head to tail, part cover, or very few plates. There is no smooth slide from one to the next and no normal distribution curve. That pattern of distinct phenotypes is the hallmark of discontinuous variation.

Link Pattern to Genes**
This happens because only one gene, EDA, with two alleles (low and high armour) is involved. A single gene gives a few clear outcomes rather than many small additive effects. The environment has little effect, so genes alone decide which box a fish falls into.
Final answer: Falls into discrete / distinct categories (complete, partial, low morphs) with no intermediates / no continuous range; controlled by only one gene (EDA) and not affected by environment.

hints: The whole freshwater lake population was destroyed in 1982, so the 1990 fish must have arrived from somewhere else. Where is the only other form of this species found, and what armour does that form normally carry?
walkthrough:
Start From an Empty Lake**
In 1982 there were no freshwater fish left in Loberg Lake, so the new fish seen in 1990 cannot be descendants of the old freshwater low-armour fish. They must be newcomers swimming in from outside.

Match the Armour to the Founder**
The newcomers almost all show head-to-tail plates. That is exactly the complete morph described as found mainly in the saltwater form for defence against large predatory fish. The simplest idea is that saltwater fish colonised the lake and brought their high-armour alleles with them.
Final answer: Saltwater / ocean fish (with complete morph) colonised the lake.

hints: Start with what must exist in any population for selection to act - do all the 1990 colonisers carry exactly the same EDA alleles?
Compare the cost and benefit of heavy bone plates in a lake versus the ocean. What does the stem tell you about calcium content, growth and predators?
Think about who leaves more offspring - a fish that wastes energy and calcium making full armour in freshwater, or one that grows larger and makes more eggs or sperm?
Follow the favourable alleles to the next generation. What happens when survivors breed?
Link the 96% to 39% drop in only three years to the type of selection and the change in allele frequency.
walkthrough:
Variation Is the Raw Material**
Even though most 1990 fish were complete morph, the population still contained genetic variation in the EDA gene, from mutation and from alleles carried by the saltwater founders. Without that variation in plate number there would be nothing to select.

Freshwater Changes the Advantage**
In the ocean, full bony plates pay off because large predatory fish are common. In a freshwater lake there are fewer large predators, and water contains little calcium needed to build bone. Full armour becomes expensive and less useful.

Fewer Plates Means More Babies**
Fish with partial or low morph alleles waste less energy and calcium making bone. The stem tells you complete armour limits growth. So low-armour fish can grow larger, lay more eggs or shed more sperm. That is the selective advantage.

Differential Survival and Inheritance**
Those better-adapted low-armour fish are more likely to survive to breeding age and reproduce. When they breed they pass their advantageous low-armour alleles to offspring. Over generations the proportion of offspring carrying those alleles rises.

Directional Change in Numbers**
That is why complete morph falls from 96% in 1990 to 39% in 1993. The allele frequency for low armour increases and for high armour decreases. Because selection pushes the whole population in one direction, away from complete toward partial and low, this is directional selection, and it can be very fast when the pressure is strong.

Final answer: Genetic variation present; selection favours fewer plates in freshwater; low-armour fish grow larger / produce more gametes / save energy and calcium; survive and reproduce more; pass on low-armour alleles so frequency of low-armour allele increases - directional selection; due to low calcium supply and fewer large predators.
